etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English certeyn, certein, certain, borrowed from Old French certain, from a Vulgar Latin unattested form *certānus, extended form of Latin certus (“fixed, resolved, certain”), of the same origin as cretus, past participle of cernere (“to separate, perceive, decide”). Displaced native Middle English wis, iwis (“certain, sure”) (from Old English ġewiss (“certain, sure”)) and alternative Middle English spelling sertane (“some, certain”).

definitions.definition: Sure in one's mind, positive; absolutely confident in the truth of something.

quote.citation: 1833, [Frederick Marryat], chapter VIII, in Peter Simple. […], volume III, London: Saunders and Otley, […], published 1834, →OCLC, page 113:
quote.text: […]  I think, nay, I may say that I'm sartain, we'll have a hurricane afore morning. It's not the first time I've cruised in these latitudes.

definitions.definition: Not to be doubted or denied; established as a fact.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Daniel 2:45, column 1:
quote.text: […] the dreame is certaine, and the interpretation thereof ſure.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, The Second Part of Henrie the Fourth, […], quarto edition, London:  […]  V[alentine] S[immes] for Andrew Wise, and William Aspley, published 1600, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: […] death (as the Pſalmiſt ſaith) is certaine to all, all ſhall die.

quote.citation: 1675, John Dryden, Aureng-zebe: A Tragedy. […], London:  […]  T[homas] N[ewcomb] for Henry Herringman, […], published 1676, →OCLC, Act II, page 29:
quote.text: How vain is Virtue which directs our ways  Through certain danger to uncertain praiſe!

quote.citation: 1702, Richard Mead, Mechanical Account of Poisons:
quote.text: I have often wished, that I knew so certain a remedy in any other disease

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Exodus 16:4, column 1:
quote.text: Then ſaid the Lord vnto Moſes, Behold, I will raine bread from heauen for you: and the people ſhall goe out, and gather a certaine rate euery day, that I may proue them, whether they will walke in my Law, or no.

definitions.definition: Particular and definite, but unspecified or unnamed; used to introduce someone or something without going into further detail.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Luke 5:12, column 1:
quote.text: And it came to paſſe, when he was in a certaine citie […]

quote.citation: 1856 February, [Thomas Babington] Macaulay, “[Contributions to the Encyclopædia Britannica.] Oliver Goldsmith.”, in T[homas] F[lower] E[llis], editor, The Miscellaneous Writings and Speeches of Lord Macaulay, new edition, London: Longman, Green, Reader, & Dyer, published 1871, →OCLC, page 365:
quote.text: About everything that he wrote, serious or sportive, there was a certain natural grace and decorum […]

definitions.definition: (euphemistic, preceded by "a") Used to denote that the speaker is referring to a specific person or thing that they do not want to name directly, implying that the listener should infer the identity of the referent.
(preceded by "a", of a person) Named but not previously mentioned.

quote.citation: 1972, Burton Pasternak, “Kinship”, in Kinship & Community in Two Chinese Villages‎[1], Stanford, CA: Stanford University Press, →ISBN, →LCCN, →OCLC, pages 75–76:
quote.text: About 140 years ago, for example, a certain Hsü Kuang-ming established an ancestral estate in Wanluan consisting of ten hectares. The trust was specifically set aside to provide for his own worship after death, and access to its profits was to be enjoyed only by his descendants.

definitions.definition: (preceded by "a", of a person) Used before the name of someone famous that people are expected to know.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book VIII”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC, lines 952–953:
quote.text: However I with thee have fixt my Lot,  Certain to undergoe like doom […]

definitions.definition: Having been determined but not specified.

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter V, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC, page 26:
quote.text: One saint's day in mid-term a certain newly-appointed suffragan-bishop came to the school chapel, and there preached on “The Inner Life.”

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Acts 23:12, column 2:
quote.text: […] certaine of the Jewes banded together […]
